name: Foundationalism
statement: Beliefs rest on a bedrock of basic beliefs that need no support from other beliefs.
statementAccent: a bedrock of basic beliefs that need no support
meaning: Foundationalism is a theory about the structure of epistemic justification, about how our justified beliefs hang together. It holds that beliefs come in two kinds. Some beliefs are basic, or foundational, meaning they have positive epistemic status, justification or knowledge, without depending on any other beliefs for that status; they are justified non-inferentially, not by being inferred from further beliefs. All other beliefs, the non-basic or superstructure beliefs, have their positive epistemic status only by depending, ultimately, on the basic ones, being justified inferentially by being supported by the foundations. The standard image is architectural: a building of beliefs resting on a foundation, in contrast to the coherentist picture of a web or raft with no privileged base. Foundationalism is chiefly a response to the regress problem of justification: if every belief must be justified by another belief, the chain of reasons threatens to run on infinitely, or to circle back on itself, and since finite reasoners cannot complete an infinite chain, foundationalism stops the regress at basic beliefs that are justified but not by anything further. The account divides into classical or strong foundationalism, which demands that basic beliefs be certain, and modest or moderate foundationalism, which allows fallible basic beliefs.
mechanism: Foundationalism answers the regress problem about the structure of justification. The problem is that a justified belief seems to need to be justified by some other belief, which in turn needs justification, and so on: the chain of reasons must either continue infinitely, turn back in a circle, or stop somewhere. Foundationalism takes the last option, holding that the chain terminates in basic beliefs that are justified non-inferentially, without depending on any further belief. These basic beliefs form the foundation; every other justified belief is a superstructure belief that inherits its status by being supported, directly or indirectly, by the foundational ones. What qualifies a belief as basic is the central question, and answers divide the view. Classical or strong foundationalism, associated with Descartes, restricts basic beliefs to those that are infallible, indubitable, or incorrigible, such as beliefs about one's own present mental states, and takes the certainty of the cogito as a model foundation; the aim is knowledge built on unshakable ground. Modest or moderate foundationalism instead allows basic beliefs that are adequately but only prima facie justified, fallible and defeasible, such as ordinary perceptual beliefs; a version called phenomenal conservatism holds that how things seem provides foundational justification unless there is a defeater. In every version, the mechanism is the same: a layer of non-inferentially justified beliefs halts the regress and grounds the rest.

examples.text: Foundationalism halts the regress of reasons at basic beliefs that are justified but not inferred from any further belief.
Classical foundationalism seeks indubitable basic beliefs, as in Descartes's certainty of his own existence, the cogito.
Non-basic beliefs form a superstructure justified by resting, ultimately, on the foundational beliefs, like a building on its base.

variants.name: Classical versus modest
variants.text: Strong foundationalism demands certain, indubitable basic beliefs; moderate foundationalism allows fallible, defeasible ones.

variants.name: Phenomenal conservatism
variants.text: A permissive modern version on which how things seem gives foundational justification unless defeated.

whyItMatters: Foundationalism is one of the two dominant theories of the structure of epistemic justification, the great rival to coherentism, and its central problem, the regress of reasons, is one of the oldest in the theory of knowledge, going back to Aristotle's Posterior Analytics. By dividing beliefs into non-inferentially justified foundations and an inferentially justified superstructure, foundationalism offers a clear and intuitive answer to the question of how justification can end without either an infinite regress or a vicious circle. The view has shaped epistemology from Aristotle and Descartes through the logical empiricists to contemporary debates, and Descartes's project of rebuilding knowledge on indubitable foundations is one of the defining moments of modern philosophy. The contrast between classical foundationalism, with its demand for certainty, and modest foundationalism, which accepts fallible foundations, frames much of the modern discussion, as does the challenge from coherentism and from Sellars's critique of the given. Even those who reject foundationalism must say how they escape the regress.

working.text: note that justifying a belief by another belief threatens an infinite regress or a circle.
hold that some beliefs are justified non-inferentially, without depending on any further belief.
justify all other beliefs by supporting them, ultimately, on the basic foundations.

limits: Foundationalism faces serious objections, several turning on the status of the basic beliefs. If a basic belief is accepted without any reason, it can look epistemically arbitrary or dogmatic, and it is fair to ask what justifies it if not another belief. Wilfrid Sellars pressed the myth of the given, sometimes cast as a dilemma: a supposedly self-justifying given either has propositional content, in which case it itself stands in need of justification and is not foundational after all, or it lacks such content, in which case it cannot justify anything; either way the idea of a self-justifying given is in trouble. Classical foundationalism faces a further problem: its demand that basic beliefs be infallible or indubitable makes the foundation so thin, restricted to beliefs about one's own mind, that building substantial knowledge of the external world or the past on it becomes very hard, inviting skepticism, which is part of why many have moved to modest foundationalism. Attribution should be handled with care, since figures such as Locke are commonly associated with the view but are best mentioned cautiously.
misreadings: Foundationalism is not the claim that basic beliefs are simply asserted without any epistemic standing; it holds they are justified non-inferentially, not by other beliefs, which its critics dispute but which is not the same as being groundless by definition. It does not require certainty, since modest foundationalism allows fallible, defeasible basic beliefs, and only classical foundationalism demands indubitability. And it is not the only answer to the regress, since coherentism and infinitism are rivals, so treating foundationalism as mere dogmatism, as committed to certainty, or as the only structural option, misreads a theory of the structure of justification.
origin: A theory of the structure of epistemic justification holding that basic beliefs are justified non-inferentially and support all other beliefs, developed as a response to the regress problem from Aristotle and Descartes onward.
